answer.rationale: The prior rollback (b1) was clean and restored stability without customer impact, so this is the highest-confidence lever for a write-path latency regression. A recent release (2h ago) is the most likely cause of a 90-minute p99 climb on writes during heavy settlement traffic, and b1 specifically shows rollback handled prior bad-build cases without losing writes. b6 (canary gating) would have been useful pre-release but is not an available intervention now. b2 (regional failover) is higher risk and unnecessary if the issue is a bad build—shifting traffic to another region carrying the same code would just move the latency spike, not fix it, and could break the 'without losing customer writes' objective during heavy settlement. Adding capacity (b3 lesson) is slower-acting than the latency climb and won't reverse a regression in the build itself. Circuit breakers (b4) fail fast and would drop writes—the opposite of the objective. Read-replica routing (b5) doesn't apply to the write path. Verifying b1 confirms the rollback procedure itself is reliable; verifying b2 keeps the regional-failover option honest in case rollback doesn't recover latency.
